extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and practitioners of combinatorics and probabilistic methods; readers interested in elegant proofs of classical combinatorial theorems
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and proofs of fundamental combinatorial theorems about families of subsets, shuffling/randomness of permutations, and a determinantal path-counting lemma. Focuses on statements, conditions, proof strategies (Lubell, Katona, stopping rules, bijections), and quantitative bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner's theorem (maximum size of an antichain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a largest antichain of an n-set is binom(n, floor(n/2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof (Lubell): count full chains ∅ = C0 ⊂ C1 ⊂ ... ⊂ Cn (there are n!); for A ∈ F with |A| = k exactly k!(n−k)! chains pass through A; no chain contains two members of an antichain; letting mk be number of k-sets in F gives sum_{k=0}^n mk k!(n−k)! ≤ n!, which reorganizes to sum_{k=0}^n mk / binom(n,k) ≤ 1 and thus |F| ≤ binom(n, floor(n/2)). Equality characterization: the family of all middle k-sets (or the two middle layers when n odd) attain the bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lubell chain-counting method
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique: count permutations/chains and how many pass through members of a family to bound family size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Sperner's theorem: compare total number of chains (n!) with sum over elements of family of number of chains through each element (k!(n−k)!). General method: pick an ensemble of combinatorial objects each member of F appears in some number of them; since overlap is restricted by property (e.g., antichain), derive inequality bounding |F|. Applicable as a versatile counting/probabilistic tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersecting family trivial bound and example
rubrics_metrics.description: For arbitrary intersecting family F of subsets of N, |F| ≤ 2^{n-1}; example achieving this is all subsets containing a fixed element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: if A ∈ F then its complement Ac cannot be in F, so at most half of all subsets can belong to an intersecting family. The family of all subsets containing a fixed element attains size 2^{n-1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem (intersecting k-families)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n ≥ 2k, the largest size of an intersecting k-family in an n-set is binom(n−1, k−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction attaining the bound: all k-sets containing a fixed element (size binom(n−1,k−1)). Proof (Katona): reduce to a geometric lemma about arcs on a circle then count appearances of k-sets as consecutive blocks in cyclic permutations. For any cyclic permutation, at most k sets of F can appear as k consecutive numbers; counting over (n−1)! cyclic permutations and dividing by k!(n−k)! appearances per set yields |F| ≤ binom(n−1,k−1). Note exceptions at n = 2k (other extremal families exist).

rubrics_metrics.name: Katona's arc lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma: Let n ≥ 2k. Given t distinct arcs of length k on an n-point circle such that any two arcs have an edge in common, then t ≤ k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: endpoints cannot be shared by more than one arc; fix one arc A1, inner endpoints of other arcs must be distinct inner points of A1 (there are k−1), so at most k arcs total. This combinatorial geometric observation is the key to Katona's proof of Erdős–Ko–Rado.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's marriage theorem (system of distinct representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection A1,...,An of subsets of a finite set X has a system of distinct representatives (SDR) iff for every m (1 ≤ m ≤ n), the union of any m of the Ai contains at least m elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition (H) (the union condition) is necessary and, remarkably, sufficient. Proof (Easterfield/Halmos–Vaughan): induction on n with the notion of a critical family (ℓ sets whose union has size ℓ) and two cases: no critical family (remove an element of An and apply induction), or existence of a critical family (solve that subcollection by induction and then solve the remainder avoiding used elements). Also mention variant: if all Ai have size k and no element lies in more than k sets, there exist k SDRs partitioning each Ai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall condition (H) as an exact criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The union of any m sets Ai contains at least m elements for all 1 ≤ m ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single combinatorial inequality is both necessary and sufficient for existence of an SDR. Useful algorithmically and conceptually (mass-wedding interpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupon collector expected time
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected number of draws with replacement to collect all n distinct coupons is n Hn = n (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n) ≈ n log n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: expected waiting time for next new coupon when k have been collected is 1/(1−k/n), sum these from k=0 to n−1 to get n Hn. Useful comparison tool when mapping other processes to coupon collector behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupon collector tail bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Vn be number of drawings to collect all n coupons. For m := ceil(n log n + c n) and c ≥ 0, Prob(Vn > m) ≤ e^{−c}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via union bound: Prob(some coupon missing after m draws) ≤ n (1−1/n)^m < n e^{−m/n} ≤ e^{−c}. Useful for high-probability upper bounds and in analyzing stopping times that mirror the coupon collector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birthday paradox collision probability formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability that n random people have all different birthdays (365 days) is p(n) = product_{i=1}^{n−1} (1 − i/365); more generally for balls into K boxes product_{i=1}^{n−1} (1 − i/K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the threshold phenomena: p(n) < 1/2 already at n = 23 for 365 days. Used to bound collision probabilities when assigning k-bit labels to n items (K = 2^k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation distance as measure of randomness
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation distance between two distributions Q1 and Q2 on Sn is ||Q1 − Q2|| := (1/2) sum_{π∈Sn} |Q1(π) − Q2(π)| = max_{S ⊆ Sn} |Q1(S) − Q2(S)|, ranges 0..1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to quantify how close a shuffle distribution is to uniform. Example: starting distribution E (identity) has ||E − U|| = 1 − 1/n!. After one top-in-at-random shuffle ||Top − U|| = 1 − 1/(n−1)!.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-in-at-random shuffle model
rubrics_metrics.description: Each step: remove the top card and insert it uniformly at random into any of the n positions (including top and bottom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to a Markov chain on Sn; very ineffective mixing (requires ~ n log n steps). Strong uniform stopping rule exists: stop when the original bottom card (labelled n) is first reinserted back into the deck — then the permutation is uniform conditional on stopping time. Analysis maps to coupon collector and gives bounds on variation distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong uniform stopping rule (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stopping rule (depending only on observed random shuffles so far) is strong uniform if for all k: when the process is stopped after exactly k steps, the resulting permutation is uniformly distributed over Sn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three useful properties: (1) such rules exist for many shuffling processes; (2) their stopping time distributions are often analyzable; (3) they provide upper bounds on variation distance via Prob(T > k). Lemma: for a process with strong uniform stopping time T, ||Q^{*k} − U|| ≤ Prob(T > k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: variation distance bounded by tail of strong uniform stopping time
rubrics_metrics.description: If a shuffling process Q has a strong uniform stopping rule with stopping time T, then for all k ≥ 0, ||Q^{*k} − U|| ≤ Prob(T > k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by conditioning on T: for any S ⊆ Sn, Q^{*k}(S) = U(S) (1 − Prob(T > k)) + Prob[Xk ∈ S | T > k] Prob(T > k), so difference from U(S) is at most Prob(T > k). This turns a tail bound on T into a bound on mixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 1 (top-in-at-random mixing bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let c ≥ 0 and k := ceil(n log n + c n). After k top-in-at-random shuffles on n cards, the variation distance satisfies d(k) := ||Top^{*k} − U|| ≤ e^{−c}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: strong uniform stopping rule for top-in-at-random maps to coupon collector; apply coupon collector tail bound and the lemma above. Interpretation: requires about n log n steps to mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riffle shuffle model (Gilbert–Shannon–Reeds model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability distribution on permutations (Rif) given equivalently by: (1) Rif(id) = (n+1)/2^n, Rif(π) = 1/2^n if π is a riffle (two interleaved increasing sequences), (2) cut t cards with probability (1/2^n) binom(n,t) then drop from right/left with probabilities r/(r+ℓ), (3) inverse view: choose random subset of cards uniformly and move them (keeping relative orders) to top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model well approximates amateur riffle shuffles and is amenable to analysis. There are 2^n − n distinct riffle permutations; inverse viewpoint convenient for analysis via binary labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse riffle shuffle labeling and stopping rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inverse riffle shuffle each card independently receives a bit 0/1; after k inverse riffle shuffles each card receives a k-bit string. Strong uniform stopping rule: STOP when all cards have distinct k-bit strings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When all k-bit labels are distinct, sorting by the binary numbers gives a uniformly random permutation (strong uniformity). Thus the stopping time T is the time until no collisions among n labels into K = 2^k bins — i.e., governed by the birthday paradox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 2 (riffle shuffle mixing bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: After k riffle shuffles on n cards, variation distance satisfies ||Rif^{*k} − U|| ≤ 1 − product_{i=1}^{n−1} (1 − i / 2^k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: analyze inverse riffle shuffles, use the stopping rule based on distinct k-bit labels; Prob(T > k) equals the collision probability from the birthday model with K = 2^k, which bounds the variation distance via the stopping-time lemma. Asymptotically need k ≈ 2 log2 n shuffles; for n = 52 the bound gives d(12) ≤ 0.28, d(14) ≤ 0.08 (but more precise analyses refine these numbers; classic result is ~7 shuffles suffices for practical randomness under refined metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reeds' inversion lemma (equivalence of forward and inverse analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: ||Rif^{*k} − U|| = ||(Rif^{-1})^{*k} − U||, so it suffices to analyze inverse riffle shuffles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because taking inverses is a bijection on permutations and U is symmetric, the variation distance is unchanged by inversion. This simplifies analysis using the labeling viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gessel–Viennot / Lindström path-determinant lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite acyclic weighted directed graph G, two n-sets of vertices A = {A1,...,An} and B = {B1,...,Bn}, and the path matrix M with mij := sum_{P: Ai→Bj} w(P), we have det M = sum_{P vertex-disjoint path systems} sign(P) w(P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: determinant equals signed weighted sum over vertex-disjoint path systems from A to B; weight of a path system is product of weights of its component paths. This generalizes the permutation expansion of determinants from bipartite/one-path-per-row contexts to arbitrary directed acyclic graphs, and is widely applicable to enumerative combinatorics problems. The proof uses a cancellation/involution argument pairing non-vertex-disjoint path systems.
